### Option 1: Formatted Contemporary Poetry (Recommended)
*This version cleans up spacing and typos, adds formal dialogue punctuation, and enhances the poetic rhythm.*

All we know of history, we learn from scenes 
in the mosaic of bone on the Senate floor: 
The Flood makes graves of the fields, 
and the angels harvest enough suffering 
to live for another thousand years. 

Moses pulls off his beard and lights a cigarette. 
*"I’m tired of pretending."* 
He pushes his box of spare commandments under his bed, 
and as he drifts to sleep, his eyes, like caves, 
fill with paintings of woolly rhinos. 

Sailing ships forest a small island. 
One light shines from a caravel—the captain’s quarters. 
It’s Christopher Columbus. 
All night he’s been sewing shrouds 
as arrival gifts for the natives. 
Little Chris presses his bleeding fingers to his mouth 
and cries quietly, *"No one appreciates me."* 

God and the Devil tuck him into bed. 
*"It’ll get better,"* they say. 
Together, they complete the shrouds for him, 
while he dreams of golden nipples. 

As it was, it is now. 
Spring translates the earth into hope— 
tongues of grass taste the sea salt on the west wind 
and the blood on soldiers’ boots. 

This morning, one of the old poets—an unkillable cockroach— 
cycled past me, yelling: 
*"You have the brightest light in America! Ha ha!"* 

On my dresser, a spider makes a web 
along the contours of my bra. 
We lie on the bed together; 
I run my hand up the muscles of your leg 
and feel its eons of evolution, 
now outlawed by the Senate.

Our entire understanding of human history derives from skeletal tiles forming a mosaic across the floor of the legislature. During the great deluge, farmland is converted into cemeteries, providing celestial beings with enough human torment to sustain their lives for another millennium. 

Detaching his artificial beard, Moses ignites a cigarette and admits he can no longer maintain his act. He slides a container of backup commandments beneath his bed frame, and as he falls asleep, his hollow, cavernous eyes fill with images of ancient cave art depicting woolly rhinoceroses.

A fleet of masted vessels stands as dense as a forest around a small islet. A single lamp illuminates the captain's room of a caravel, where Christopher Columbus sits. He has spent the entire night stitching funeral shrouds to hand out as greeting gifts to the native people. Suckling his punctured, bleeding fingers, young Chris weeps quietly, complaining that nobody appreciates his efforts. The Almighty and Satan join together to tuck him into bed, offering comfort by assuring him that his situation will improve. While Columbus reposes and dreams of gilded breasts, God and the devil work side by side to finish sewing the burial garments.

The present remains an exact reflection of the past. The arrival of spring converts the landscape into a statement of hope, as individual blades of grass taste both the ocean salt swept in by western gusts and the gore staining combatants' footwear. 

Earlier today, an elderly poet—resembling an indestructible cockroach—pedaled a bicycle past me, laughingly exclaiming that I possess the most radiant glow in the nation. Indoors, upon my chest of drawers, an arachnid constructs its web along the outline of my brassiere. Reclining beside you on the mattress, I stroke the muscular length of your leg, perceiving millions of years of natural adaptation that have recently been declared illegal by the government.

From a distant, cosmic perspective, human history reveals itself not as a linear march toward enlightenment, but as an endless cycle of suffering and political decay. Empires rise and collapse in predictable, agonizing rhythms, generating a dark energy that seems to feed powerful, unseen forces hovering just beyond the veil of mortal comprehension. Age after age, the machinery of war and statecraft grinds ordinary lives into dust, extracting their vitality to fuel a grand, tragic spectacle.

This relentless machinery wears down even the greatest architects of human destiny. In the quiet solitude of the desert, Moses is reimagined not as a triumphant leader, but as an exhausted, sun-beaten man broken by the weight of his calling. Desperate to escape his persona, he buries a set of unused commandments deep beneath the sand—truths too gentle or too heavy for a restless world—and casts aside his prophet’s staff. Stripping off the heavy mantle of divine duty, he simply lies down in the shade of a barren rock, choosing peaceful oblivion over eternal myth.

Centuries later, the same haunting futility shadows the age of expansion. Christopher Columbus sits in the humid gloom of the New World, a tearful, unappreciated figure stripped of his historical glory. Realizing the devastating cost of his ambition, he spends his final hours weeping as he sews death shrouds for the native people whose world he helped destroy. In this grim, surreal task, he is aided by an eerie celestial partnership: God holds the white linen smooth while the devil pulls the thread taut, both divine and infernal powers colluding in the tragic undoing of innocence.

Yet, despite the endless trail of human carnage, the natural world maintains its stubborn rhythm. Every year, spring returns to renew the earth, blanketing scarred battlefields in vibrant greenery and blooming flowers that whisper promises of hope. Beneath the surface, the soil quietly absorbs the blood spilled by generations of soldiers, integrating the tragic waste of human life into the tapestry of the ecosystem. Nature forgives what humanity cannot, turning crimson battlegrounds into quiet meadows.

It is ultimately in the quietest, most vulnerable spaces that the human spirit reclaims its power. Away from the grand narratives of history, an intimate moment of physical connection between two people reveals a profound truth. As skin meets skin in a tender embrace, the raw, beautiful reality of human evolution comes into sharp relief—proving that the instinct for love and genuine connection will always transcend, outlast, and defy the cold, restrictive laws written by distant senates.

**I. The Broken Monuments**

Consider Columbus on the shore of his own mind,
not cast in bronze, but shivering in wet velvet,
coughing up red dust and sea glass,
his compass spinning wildly toward a bank of fog.
His hands, which signed away a hemisphere,
now fumble with the buttons of a damp coat,
terrified of the dark water he summoned.

And Moses, high on the gravelly ridge of Nebo,
is not a giant carved from marble.
He is a old man with sun-cracked lips and swollen knees,
weeping over the heavy limestone slabs
that bruised his shoulders for forty years.
He looks down at the valley and sees not milk and honey,
but the endless, rolling smoke of burning fields,
the golden calves melted down into bayonets,
the endless march of hungry children
walking from one barbed border to the next.

This is the alchemy of the palace and the pulpit:
to take the bruised, trembling flesh of kings and prophets
and dip it in gold leaf,
so no one smells the iron in the dirt,
so no one hears the quiet, choking sound of history
repeating its old, blood-soaked script.

**II. The Edicts of the Realm**

In the marble halls of the capital,
men who have forgotten the smell of rain
draw red lines across the ribs of the earth.
They draft decrees to render breathing illegal,
to categorize the sunrise, to outlaw the body,
to declare that tenderness without a permit
is an act of treason against the state.

They build museums to house their massacres
and name the quiet avenues after the men who cleared them.
Empire is a machine that eats the present
and vomits up a sanitized past,
a museum guard insisting
that the blood on the carpet is merely part of the design.

**III. What Endures**

Yet, past the police lines and the iron gates,
in a third-floor apartment bathed in early light,
you turn in your sleep and stretch your arm across the sheet.
Your skin is warm, untouched by the morning news.
I watch the slow, rhythmic rise of your chest,
more absolute than any constitutional law,
more real than the charter of any forgotten king.

Outside the window, a dandelion breaks through three inches of asphalt,
yellow head defying the concrete weight of the city.
The sparrows do not register the redrawn maps;
they nest in the hollow eyes of forgotten statues.

Let the empires print their currencies and erect their obelisks.
Let the tribunals outlaw the shape of our longing.
Here, in the quiet shade of this kitchen,
where the coffee drips and your hand finds mine,
the mythologies of power crumble back into sand.
The state may own the memory of the dead,
but the living—stubborn, soft, and ungovernable—
still belong to the morning.

**Title:** The Chamber of Representation: Understanding the Senate

Throughout the history of democratic governance, few institutions hold as much weight and authority as **the** **Senate**. Originating in ancient Rome from the Latin word *senatus*—meaning a council of elders—the concept has evolved into a modern cornerstone of legislative power across **all** corners of the globe.

In many bicameral systems, such as that of the United States, **the** **Senate** serves as a crucial counterweight to the lower legislative house. While population dictates representation in the lower chamber, **the** upper body grants equal stature to **all** regions, regardless of their geographical size or economic output. This intentional design ensures that less populous areas are not silenced by larger ones, fostering a system where **all** states or provinces have a voice in shaping national policy.

**The** responsibilities entrusted to **the** **Senate** carry immense weight. Beyond standard lawmaking, senators are often tasked with high-stakes duties: confirming executive appointments, approving international treaties, and overseeing impeachment trials. When **all** members gather on **the** chamber floor to cast their votes, their decisions resonate far beyond the capitol building. Every bill passed and treaty ratified holds the potential to impact **all** citizens within the nation.

Ultimately, **the** **Senate** stands as an enduring symbol of deliberation and balance. By requiring representatives from **all** backgrounds to negotiate, debate, and compromise, it serves to protect **the** foundational principles of stability, justice, and rule of law for the entire country.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, darkly humorous free-verse poem about the tragedy and absurdity of human history. Include scenes where Moses drops his act to smoke a cigarette, Christopher Columbus cries while sewing shrouds as gifts for indigenous people, and a modern intimate scene where evolution has been outlawed by the Senate.
counterfactuals.output:
History is a meat grinder fitted with a brass band.
We dragged ourselves out of the primordial soup
only to discover we owed back taxes on the mud.

High on Sinai, the burning bush was losing its leaves,
sputtering like a wet match in the desert wind.
The thunder groaned its last mandatory rumble,
and God stepped behind a jagged crag to take a call.
Moses let his shoulders drop six inches.
The heavy stone tablets clattered against his shin.
He reached deep into the sweat-stained hem of his robe,
pulled out a crushed pack of menthols,
and struck a light off a hot coal from the bush.
He took a long, ragged drag, squinting down at the valley
where the boys were already melting their fillings into a calf.
“Ten,” he muttered, exhaling a blue ribbon of smoke
that curled into a tiny dollar sign.
“I could’ve given them three, and they’d still be sleeping with the goats.”

Empire is just a sequence of heavy men
choking on chicken bones while painters render their chins.

Consider the Admiral of the Ocean Sea.
The moon over Hispaniola hangs like a peeled turnip.
Inside his cabin, Christopher Columbus sits by a sputtering lamp,
sniffling, his face flushed and greasy with fever.
He is weeping—real, fat, heartbroken tears—
as he works a silver needle through bolts of fine Flemish linen.
He is sewing shrouds.
He trims the edges with delicate crimson lace,
folding them into neat, square gift parcels,
tied with silk ribbons.
“They have such gentle eyes,” he sobs, wiping his nose on his velvet sleeve,
stitching another tiny shroud for a child he hasn't met yet.
“It breaks my heart, really it does. 
They aren't going to survive the salvation I brought them.”
He drops a tear onto the bleached cloth;
the salt stain expands like an island on a map.

Time, that stupid dog, keeps fetching its own thrown stick.
We marched through the Age of Reason
and straight into the air-conditioned tribunal.

Now, in apartment 4B, the radiator clanks its bronze teeth.
I lay my hand on the small of your back,
right where our ancestors kept their balance in the canopy.
We kiss quietly, terrified of the shadows on the blinds.
At midnight, the Senate passed the Stasis Act:
*An Ordinance to Outlaw the Transgressions of Natural Selection.*
It is now a federal offense to mutate.
Our vestigial tailbones are under court order to remain useless.
If your blood attempts to adapt to the microplastics,
the bailiff will confiscate your liver.
We hold each other in the dark, motionless,
trying to suppress the urge to grow gills
as the sea level creeps up the fire escape.
“Don’t change,” you whisper, and it’s not a romantic plea—
it’s a warning.
If we accidentally synthesize a new enzyme mid-orgasm,
the C-SPAN cameras will know.

Oh, grand parade of the upright ape!
We built cathedrals out of spit and fever,
carved our names into the bark of a dying world,
and locked the doors from the inside
just in case the monkeys came back to ask for their thumbs.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an absurdist, cynical poem about how history repeats its cruelties, connecting biblical times, the Age of Discovery, and present-day America by making famous historical and religious figures seem petty, tired, or pathetic.
counterfactuals.output:
The Almighty sits in a mildewed lawn chair,
Picking at a scab, nursing a mild headache.
He regrets the oceans; the fish are too loud.
Moses is whining about a blister on his heel,
Muttering, "Why couldn't the burning bush just text?"
Down in the valley, Pharaoh is throwing a tantrum
Because the frog plague didn't match his curtains.
Pontius Pilate scrubs his cuticles raw with a toothbrush,
Stressed about his cholesterol, annoyed by the crowd,
While three poor bastards get nailed to wood beams
Like cheap flyers stapled to a telephone pole.

Shift the reel forward: the vomit hits the deck.
Christopher Columbus is rubbing his heat rash,
Gasping on a salted turnip, utterly lost,
Squinting through a spyglass made of cheap brass.
"Is this India?" he snivels, wiping his nose on his sleeve,
"I don't care, take their gold, chop off their thumbs,
I need to pay off my mortgage in Seville."
In Madrid, King Ferdinand has gout in his big toe;
Queen Isabella trades smallpox blankets for shiny beads,
Then eats cold porridge and gossips about the Pope,
Who is currently selling indulgences to fund his nephew’s bad poetry.

Now the wheel rolls into a modern strip mall parking lot.
Uncle Sam sits in a idling sedan, drooling on his necktie,
Eating cold French fries, waiting for the climate to end.
A billionaire in a fleece vest sits on a golden toilet,
Doomscrolling through footage of a wedding getting droned,
Complaining that the wifi in his bunker is a little spotty.
The Senate is just sixty men named Bob,
Sharing one tired brain cell, arguing over a parking space,
While the police force buys a tank to fight a teenager with a skateboard.

It’s the same dull guillotine, just with a touchscreen.
The torture rack now comes with ergonomic lumbar support.
Moses, Columbus, and a guy in a MAGA hat
Are all standing in line at the same greasy buffet,
Complaining that the meat is tough,
Passing the same bloody baton,
Crushing the exact same toes in the exact same mud,
Forever, and ever,
Adjusting the thermostat while the planet smells like burnt toast.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the style of modern avant-garde surrealism. Elements to incorporate: a mosaic of bone, Moses hiding spare commandments under his bed, God and the Devil tucking Columbus into bed, an old poet riding a bicycle, and a spider on a bra.
counterfactuals.output:
The city ground its pavement into a mosaic of bone,
tessellated kneecaps and fused ribs humming beneath the frost.
Over this calcified grid, an old poet rides a bicycle;
his tires are inflated with the last breath of a dying dialect,
his rusty spokes slicing the fog into ribbons of wet grease.

Upstairs, where the walls are wallpapered in salt,
Moses kneels beside his brass bedstead.
Sweeping away dust bunnies made of locust wings,
he shoves the spare commandments under the mattress—
stone slabs still soft as unbaked dough,
inscribed with secret, forbidden syntax:
*Thou shalt not measure the shadow of bread,*
*Thou shalt forgive the geometry of the wolf.*

Down the hall of infinite, restless tides,
the nursery of empires smells of sulfur and lavender.
God pulls the thick wool blanket up to Columbus’s chin,
while the Devil fluffs the pillow of raw spices,
tucking the small, feverish explorer into bed.
"Sleep now, little sailor," they sing in a two-part harmony,
"the earth is flat enough to catch your falls."

Outside, suspended between two electricity poles,
a black lace bra sways like a sleeping stingray.
At the apex of the left cup,
a velvet spider sits quietly,
weaving an eighth leg out of moonlight,
listening to the beat of a phantom breast.

The poet pedals faster into the blinding static.
The bone tiles click underfoot.
The sky unbuttons its third eye, and rains down teeth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dreamlike, surrealist poem about human nature, blending mythic scale with mundane domestic details. Make it feel dark, satirical, and poetic.
counterfactuals.output:
We were forged from primordial magma and dishwater,
poured into the gentle cycle of an endless Tuesday.
Atlas stands by the avocado-green counter,
his spine popping like worn laminate,
holding up a heavens-full of unwashed mugs.

Every morning, the sun is dragged across the sky
by four blind horses made of Tupperware.
We swallow the dawn with two sugars and skim milk,
then complain that the glare ruins the television.
In the hallway closet, behind the winter coats,
the Sphinx sits brooding on a pile of lone socks,
asking riddles no one hears over the hum of the fridge:
*“What walks on four legs, then two, then refinances?”*
The mold in the corner whispers: *Us. Always us.*

We conquered the atom just to warm a slice of ham.
We mapped the cosmic web, then lost the TV remote.
Prometheus is chained to the radiator in the basement;
the eagle arrives precisely at three fifteen,
wipes its beak on the laundry hamper,
and stays to complain about the price of gas.

Icarus did not melt from the heat of the sun—
he caught a draft from the central air,
his wax wings chattering, snapping like brittle plastic
over the beige carpet of the master bedroom.

Look at us: god-husked, clay-brained, magnificent parasites.
We construct Babel out of Amazon boxes,
reach for the infinite,
and weep because the Wi-Fi dropped its signal to the stars.

And when the end comes, delivered by certified mail,
we will be standing in the kitchen at midnight,
bathed in the pale, holy light of an open refrigerator,
searching for our immortal souls
behind a jar of expired mayonnaise—
while the universe spins slowly on a microwave turntable,
unevenly thawed,
and still ice-cold at the center.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a piece of poetry that contrasts grand historical narratives with bizarre, intimate surrealism? I want it to critique human history and politics while ending on a sensual yet dystopian note.
counterfactuals.output:
The mapmakers dipped their quills in goose fat and gravity,
drawing red lines through kitchens, slicing beds in two.
Alexander wept because his horse turned into a choir of crickets,
and Caesar sat in the forum, his marble stomach full of warm stew
and the clipped fingernails of forgotten slaves.
We were told the narrative was a staircase of bronze, ascending—
that the blood in the gutters was merely oil for the grand clockwork.

Instead, the Senate debates the weight of the sun,
voting unanimously to outlaw the color blue,
while beneath the mahogany table, a junior minister 
secretly feeds his third eye a crust of damp bread.
We traded the wilderness for a receipt printed on linen.
We built cathedrals out of calcified teeth and microchips,
then raised our hand-drawn flags to scream at the rain for a discount.

Now, the Great War is fought with polished spoons in an alleyway.
Generals wearing suits woven from boiled smoke 
declare victory over the concept of Tuesday.
The news anchor’s smile detaches from her face,
floating toward the camera like a pale, wet moth.
Progress was only a train that ate its own tracks to build the next mile,
leaving us here, in the grand, rusted belly of the machine.

So lock the door against the parliament of ash.
Let the empire rot into the carpet.
Come lie beside me on this mattress of decaying feathers,
where the neon from the dead neon sign drips like warm butter.

Touch the small of my back; my skin tastes of zinc and lavender syrup.
Outside, the last satellite falls like a burning swan,
redrawing the sky in a flash of dying violet,
but inside, your mouth is a dark, humid room where history goes to drown.
I press my tongue to the soft hollow of your throat,
counting your pulse—a tiny, terrified animal trapped in a velvet glove.

The world bleeds black oil into the floorboards.
We press our ribcages together until they click like cool gears,
whispering manifestos into each other’s collarbones,
tangled, radioactive, and exquisitely undone.
